name: Zoe Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. Your answers are confidential; what does an ordinary day building or repairing power lines involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a crew for the electricity company, and my day begins with permits, a truck inventory and choosing who checks each isolation. My technical diploma matters, but the knack is hearing a colleague say something feels wrong and stopping before we touch the line.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What has changed in your own routine, and what keeps you here?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use AI every day to sort fault photos and draft handovers, then compare its text with the signed sheet. I like getting the crew safely home; my partner Luis and I have two school-age children, a mortgage and more than six months saved, so I can enjoy the work without counting every shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew a faster report is welcome if the person who tested the line still signs it. The small AI tools I use already help me find yesterday’s fault photos without pretending to inspect today’s pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel lucky that our higher lineworker pay and savings give us room. I would not buy a machine just because someone promises to save ten minutes of paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep using my checked AI handovers and my crew’s signed permit routine. In the first year I’d test the company’s new photo sorting feature on old, closed jobs before bringing it into a live shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm and a bit curious. Routine help is pleasant when it does not move the safety decision away from the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the photo feature useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would have to find the correct pole and date without mixing two repair jobs. I would reject it after a repeated mismatch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would check the sorted photos before a live shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the output myself against our job numbers and ask another crew lead to spot-check a sample. A tidy AI fault-photo album is not proof of a safe power line.

say: **AI photo sorting** can save time on old fault records.
The person who **tested the line** must still sign the permit.
think: Our **higher pay** and reserve make a small technology change easy to absorb.
I would not **buy equipment** for a ten-minute paperwork promise.
do: **Continue** checked AI handovers and signed crew permits.
**Test** the new photo sorting feature on closed jobs before live use.
feel: **Calm** about the job and curious about a limited tool.
S0.quote: A tidy AI fault-photo album is not proof of a safe power line.
fieldNote: She already uses **AI daily** but insists that actual test results govern a line permit.
Her trial uses **closed jobs**, avoiding claims that software can inspect a live pole.

steps.text: Continue checked AI handovers and signed permits
Test AI photo sorting on closed repair jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say dispatch may get much faster at planning and buying, while a crew still needs to build and repair lines. I would volunteer for a ticket pilot so the field errors reach the software team before crews lose time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my line job feels fairly secure, but I worry the company will use quick scheduling to expect an extra job after dark. Good pay does not make a tired crew safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the dispatch lead for a place in the ticket pilot next month and compare its parts lists with five recent repair sites. During the first year I’d learn the new planning screen and send back every missing connector with its job number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about pace, not frightened for my wages. A pilot gives me a way to shape the handover rather than just accept it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pilot saves travel but adds another call?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask how much time remains for testing and isolation before accepting the extra call. A shorter drive to a line repair does not make the conductor less live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What information would you send with a missing connector?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d send the ticket number, the part listed, the part actually needed and a photo from the site. The software team could then see which rule failed.

say: **Dispatch planning** and buying may change before physical line repairs.
I would join a **ticket pilot** to correct field errors.
think: Quick **scheduling** could add a late call and leave crews tired.
My own **lineworker wage** still looks secure in this picture.
do: **Join** the dispatch ticket pilot if accepted next month.
**Learn** its planning screen and report missing connectors with job numbers.
feel: **Uneasy** about crew pace, while confident in continued paid work.
S1.quote: A shorter drive to a line repair does not make the conductor less live.
fieldNote: Her **high skill** and daily AI use lead her to seek a practical pilot, not a wholesale career change.
She tests a concrete **trade-off**: travel time saved against time left for safe isolation.

steps.text: Join the dispatch ticket pilot if accepted
Report missing connectors with job numbers during the pilot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew full thinking AI by 2028 could plan nearly everything, but people still do line repairs until capable robots arrive around 2031. I want the electricity company to show how a crew stops a robot that misreads a pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my lead experience and our savings buy choices, though a robot that can work as well as us may eventually shrink crews. There are plenty of other lineworker jobs nearby, so I would not panic over one company’s trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask to observe a supervised robot trial on a dead line and learn its stop control before 2028 if the company offers access. I’d also review nearby utility vacancies once a quarter and put another two hundred monthly from regular pay into our reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the possible crew cut, but not trapped. We could carry the mortgage for months while I looked for a suitable paid post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you test at the dead-line trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the machine to handle a cracked crossarm that differs from its drawing and watch whether it stops safely. I would not treat a polished robot video as a field test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually apply elsewhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would apply if my company announced a real lead cut and another utility offered comparable pay and travel. Until then, I would keep earning here and keep the vacancy list current.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes planning before line-capable robots arrive around 2031.
I would demand a **stop control** that crews can use beside a misread pole.
think: My **lead skills**, strong reserve and nearby employers give choices if crews shrink.
The risk to my **current job** is real once robots reach physical repair work.
do: **Learn** the stop control at a supervised dead-line robot trial before 2028 if company access is offered.
**Review** nearby utility vacancies each quarter, applying only after real cuts and a suitable offer.
**Save** two hundred monthly from regular pay into the reserve.
feel: **Anxious** about crew cuts, though savings and local jobs leave control.
S2.quote: I would not treat a polished robot video as a field test.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **2028 planning change** from hands-on robot capability around 2031.
Her job move depends on an **actual cut** and comparable pay and travel; new saving comes from future wages.

steps.text: Learn stop control at supervised dead-line robot trial before 2028 if access offered
Review utility vacancies and apply if cuts and suitable offer occur
Save two hundred monthly from regular pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my crew thinking AI in 2031 and capable line robots around 2034 give us time to test through more than one storm season. I would want experienced repair crews involved in the trial design.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I could lead a robot inspection team if it becomes a paid role, and I would enjoy learning the equipment. Yet I do not know whether that post will exist or whether it would pay as well as my crew lead job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d ask the training lead which funded equipment module is planned and request a place if the company offers paid practice. I’d collect the faults our crew finds that drawings missed and use them in any trial design meeting I am invited to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel curious and mostly calm. Five years lets me test the work and the pay before leaving a good post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What fault would you put into a trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d use a water-damaged joint that looks sound from a distance and see what the robot reports. The crew should be allowed to challenge the machine’s answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you enrol before knowing the inspection pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take a funded module with paid practice while keeping my current shifts, but I would not accept a new post without its pay terms. Our mortgage does not run on interesting robot inspection titles.

say: **2031 thinking AI** precedes capable line robots around 2034 and allows longer field trials.
Experienced crews should help design **robot tests**.
think: A paid **inspection lead** post might suit me if one exists.
I need actual **pay terms** before leaving a good crew lead wage.
do: **Request** a funded equipment module with paid practice if offered.
**Collect** faults missed by drawings for any invited trial meeting.
**Keep** current crew shifts while testing a training path.
feel: **Curious** and mostly calm with time to check work and pay.
S3.quote: Our mortgage does not run on interesting robot inspection titles.
fieldNote: She is willing to take **funded practice** while retaining her current job, then assess a real offer.
The **fault examples** would test a robot’s physical inspection, not merely its paperwork.

steps.text: Request and take funded equipment training if paid practice is offered
Collect drawing-missed faults for any invited trial meeting
Keep current crew shifts while testing the training path

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues thinking AI in 2036 and capable robots around 2039 leave a decade for thoughtful testing. We can make the repair record good enough to compare machine work with what experienced crews actually find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be in my fifties when line robots arrive, so a less physical inspection role could be welcome. If no paid role appears, there are other electricity crews nearby and I still have a useful trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I’d build a labelled photo bank of unusual faults from completed jobs and invite two crew leads to check it. I’d continue my daily AI notes and ask the company to include those photos in future equipment trials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the long lead time. I can help write the checks and decide later whether inspection work suits my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a photo useful to a future trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The photo needs a date, pole number, test result and the repair we actually made. Otherwise the machine might learn the wrong lesson from a pretty picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if another crew lead disagrees with the label?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put both views and the final test result in the record, then let the trial team see the disagreement. A labelled line-fault bank should not hide uncertainty.

say: **2036 thinking AI** and robots around 2039 leave time to compare machines with actual line repairs.
I would build a **fault photo bank** from completed jobs.
think: A less physical **inspection role** could fit my fifties if it pays properly.
Nearby **electricity crews** remain an option if no such role appears.
do: **Build** a labelled photo bank from completed line repairs.
**Invite** two crew leads to check fault labels and test results.
**Continue** daily AI notes and ask for photo use in future trials.
feel: **Calm** with time to improve records and make a later career decision.
S4.quote: A labelled line-fault bank should not hide uncertainty.
fieldNote: Her long-term plan turns current **AI note skills** into a carefully checked repair record.
She preserves **disagreement** beside test results rather than pretending a robot-ready label is always certain.

steps.text: Build and check a labelled photo bank of completed repairs
Continue checked daily AI fault notes
Ask the company to use photo records in future trials

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because the jump from planning software to capable line robots is quick even for a willing learner. Supervised dead-line tests, a real crew stop control and honest staffing numbers would help us decide what to learn next.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks a robot’s repair after the truck has gone. A restored light is not proof that a connector will survive the next storm.

headlineQuote: A restored light is not proof that a connector will survive the next storm.
portrait: Zoe is a skilled **line crew lead** with a technical diploma, higher pay, two children, a mortgage and over six months saved.
She uses **AI daily** for notes and fault photos while checking every claim against signed permits and field tests.
Fast line robots make her **anxious** about crew size, though nearby jobs and savings give her choices.
With more time, she would test **funded inspection training** and build a checked fault photo bank.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time between changed planning and line-capable robots around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Supervised **dead-line tests**, a crew stop control and honest staffing numbers would help her plan training.
